???
Als je de gof print, dan zie je een hele serie tabellen. Bijv. voor esp.
Elke rij geeft aan het aantal esp dat in de data en/of de gesimuleerde netwerken
voorkwam. In dit geval zijn dat minimaal 0 en maximaal 19.

In de plot: de grijze boxen geven de verdeling van de % esp met een bepaalde waarde
die in de gesimuleerde netwerken voor kwam. Bijv.: bereken voor elke simulatie het
percentage edges met esp = 0. Dan geeft dan een verdeling van percentages over de
simulaties heen.
Voor de observaties staat het gemiddelde % over de de observeerde nw's vermeld (je hebt
immers meerdere tijdstippen waarop het nw is geobserveerd). Zo ook de mediaan, etc.

In de tabel: hier staan de %. Dus, het gem % edges met esp = 0 is 13.965%.

De p--waarden geven aan welk % van de gesimuleerde waarden kleiner zijn dan de geobserveerde
waarde. Dus, p = .234 voor esp = 0 betekent dat 23% van de gesimuleerde netwerken
een kleiner % edges hebben met esp = 0 dan in de observatie.
Als die p erg klein is, bijv,. bij esp = 6 t/m esp = 17, dan is de waarde in het gesimuleerde
netwerk dus bijna altijd groter dan in de geobserveerde graaf. Ofwel: je overschat
het effect structureel.
Bij p = 1 heb je ws die waarde nooit in de gesimuleerde gezien, terwijl die wel in de
observatie zit...?

In de plot: de gestippelde lijn is de gemiddelde waarde in de observaties, de
dikke lijn de mediaan.




==== ROC 
TPR = of all 1's in the data, which proportion do you correctly predict as 1
FPR = of all 0's in the data, which proportion do you incorrectly predict as 1

ROC curve: TPR vs FPR

FRP: you want this really low (x-axis)
TPR: you want this really high (y-axis

so: curve all the way in top left corner

--> Measures the model's ability to distinguish between 1's and 0's without considering distribution. of 1's and 0's​

Best suited for balanced datasets, where the number of 1's and 0's is similar.


==== PR (precision-recall) 
Precision = of all predicted 1's, which proportion is correct
Recall = TPR

PR curve: Precision op y-as, Recall op x-as
Precision: wil je zo hoog mogelijk, dus hoog op y-as
Recall: wil je hoog, dus hoog op x-as

So, you want the curve all the way in the top right corner

--> Measures the accuracy of positive predictions and the model’s ability to find positive instances.​

Best suited for imbalanced datasets — where 1's are rare, PR curves give more insights into real model performance.

=====
Practical Differences
ROC curves can look “good” even if the model performs poorly on the minority class, because the bulk of negatives can dominate FPR.

PR curves reveal weak performance on the positive class, making them more informative in scenarios like fraud detection or disease diagnosis, where the positive class is rare.


---
# Intermezzo: rusty on ROC and PR?

.b.Red-inline[ROC: plots FPR (False Positive Rate, x-axis) against TPR (True Positive Rate, y-axis)]

TPR = fraction of ties that are correctly predicted by the model

FPR = faction of 0's in the data that are incorrectly predicted as 1

You want TPR to be very high and FPR to be very low. 
Hence: the curve should lean strongly into the top-left corner of the plot, this 
indicates how well the model can distinguish between 1's and 0's in the networks.

(the ROC of a poor model will be close to the diagonal)

_Best suited for balanced datasets, where the number of 1's and 0's is similar._
<br><br>
.b.Red-inline[PR: plots TPR (True Positive Rate, x-axis) against Precision (y-axis)]

Precision = of all predicted 1's, which proportion is correct

You want TPR and Precision to be very high. 
Hence: the curve should lean strongly into the top-right corner

_Best suited for imbalanced datasets — where 1's are rare_

(a poor model will just mimic the network's density horizontally)

# Model III: out-of-sample GOF


.panelset[

.panel[.panel-name[R Code]
```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
model.03 <- btergm::btergm(friendship[1:3] ~ edges + mutual + ttriple +
                     transitiveties + ctriple + nodeicov("idegsqrt") + nodeicov("odegsqrt") +
                     nodeocov("odegsqrt") + nodeofactor("sex") + nodeifactor("sex") +
                     nodematch("sex") + edgecov(primary) + delrecip() +
                     memory(type = "stability"), R = 100)

# out of sample gof
gof.03 <- btergm::gof(model.03, nsim = 100, target = friendship[[4]],
              formula = friendship[3:4] ~ edges + mutual + ttriple +
                transitiveties + ctriple + nodeicov("idegsqrt") +
                nodeicov("odegsqrt") + nodeocov("odegsqrt") + nodeofactor("sex") +
                nodeifactor("sex") + nodematch("sex") + edgecov(primary) +
                delrecip + memory(type = "stability"),
              statistics = c(btergm::esp, btergm::dsp, btergm::geodesic, 
                             btergm::deg, btergm::triad.undirected, btergm::rocpr))
```
]



.panel[.panel-name[GOF of out of sample network]
.font70.scroll-box-24[
```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
plot(gof.03)
```


]
]

]

name: interpret
description: the probability of a tie

# The probability of an edge

Get all probabilities using `btergm::edgeprob(model.03)`

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
ep <- btergm::edgeprob(model.03)
```

Extract what you need:

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
ep[ep$i == 10 & ep$j == 15 & ep$t == 2, "probability"]
ep[ep$i == 10 & ep$j %in% c(9, 11, 12, 15) & ep$t == 2, "probability"]
```

Note: you  can also use `btergm::interpret`.

.panelset[

.panel[.panel-name[R Code]
What is the probability of an edge between _i_ and _j_ if 

* there is no tie from _j_ to _j_

* the actors have a different gender

* attended a different primary school

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
btergm::summary(model.04)
```
]


.panel[.panel-name[Summary]
.scroll-box-36[

In this case _mutual_ = _nodematch.sex_ = _edgecov.primary[[i]]_ = 0.
So, the logodds of this tie is -3.0875.

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
1 / (1 + exp(+3.0875))

plogis(-3.0875)

```

Note: this is the overall probability for this tie  across the four waves.

]
]
]

.panel[.panel-name[R Code]
